schools.summary: Gill has him leave home because a man of spirit could not bear contempt nor live in dependence on others, and notes that Gilead took a lawful wife only after Jephthah was born.

Henry reports the guesses about the mother without settling them, Josephus making Jephthah a stranger on that side and the Jews an Ishmaelite, and insists that no man ought to be reproached with the infelicities of his parentage while he labours by his own merits to roll the reproach away; he sees rigour rather than legality in the expulsion, notes the double edge of a statute that shut out Ammonites and the base-born in the same breath, and defends the men who joined him as going out to hunt and to raid land Israel had a title to rather than to rob.

Clarke would render the word for the mother hostess rather than harlot, citing the Targum, which calls her a keeper of a tavern, and thinks her a Canaanite, which he makes the real ground of the expulsion; he reads the followers as empty men wanting sense, though allowing the word may mean only men without property.

Ellicott holds harlot the only possible rendering, since all the versions give it and a word for an inferior wife was available and unused, notes that the expulsion agreed with the law and with old family practice, and calls Jephthah simply a sort of Syrian freebooter whose half-heathen origin worked on him as it had on Abimelech; Keil and Delitzsch insist that Gilead is a real man and not the country personified, the name of a famous ancestor being repeated in a descendant.

debates.question: What does the word used of Jephthah’s mother mean?

sides.position: harlot — every version gives it, and the word for an inferior wife was available and not used
a hostess or tavern-keeper, as the Targum has it, and very probably a Canaanite

debates.question: What were the men who gathered to him?

sides.position: freebooters on predatory expeditions, after the manner of Bedouins
ruined men who went out to hunt, and perhaps to raid land Israel had a title to, but not to rob

themes: the son of an harlot
thou shalt not inherit in our father’s house
the land of Tob
vain men gathered to him

schools.summary: Gill reads caution into the offer, since they did not propose to make him king, Abimelech having taught them what that came to, and said nothing of his being judge, a judge being raised up by God and not chosen by the people.

Henry marks the reversal, that many days after Jephthah was thrust out in disgrace he was fetched back with honour, and that the elders came in person meaning to take no denial; he presses the principle that magistrates who can protect the injured and neglect to redress their grievances are really guilty of inflicting them, finds the whole case a resemblance of Israel's own with God, and draws two lessons — never to trample on a man because he is mean, and for men of worth who are slighted to leave it to God to bring their light out of obscurity.
Clarke recalls that the command had already been offered to anyone who would take it, and takes the elders' answer at face value as a confession of injustice.

Ellicott measures the interval by the man, from his expulsion in early youth to his mature manhood, and finds the repetition significant, since an invasion introduced as though it were news suggests the writer had turned to a new and probably Gileadite source; Keil and Delitzsch observe that Jephthah lays his expulsion at the door of the elders although only his brothers drove him out, which does not prove the act illegal but shows that he thought it so.

themes: come and be our captain
did not ye hate me and expel me
why are ye come unto me now
therefore we turn again to thee

9.pericope_label: The bargain and the oath at Mizpeh

schools.summary: Gill sees the reason for the bargain in Jephthah's history, since a man used as he had been, and knowing how fickle men are once their turn is served, would want the terms settled beforehand.

Clarke follows the three stages by which the appointment was made complete: the elders chose him, the people confirmed the choice, and God was brought in as a party when Jephthah repeated his terms before the Lord.

Ellicott declines to defend the transaction as patriotism, Jephthah being only half an Israelite and long resident among heathens and outlaws, and quotes the judgment that where Gideon is the highest pitch this period reaches, Jephthah and Samson are the lowest points to which it descends; he answers the view that the oath was sworn before the ark by observing that the western Mizpeh would have been named had it been meant, and that the high priest was unlikely to carry the sacred lots into a threatened district. Keil and Delitzsch resist reading Jephthah's words as a question at all, since the reply according to thy words presupposes a statement, and deny flatly that the ark was present, the eastern tribes having none.

debates.question: Does “before the Lord” imply the ark was at Mizpeh?

sides.position: no — the eastern tribes had no ark, and the words imply only that Jephthah confirmed his terms by an oath
probably not — the western Mizpeh would have been specified, and the phrase means only some solemn religious act

themes: shall I be your head
the Lord be witness between us
the people made him head and captain
before the Lord in Mizpeh

12.pericope_label: The embassy and the Ammonite claim

schools.summary: Gill thinks Jephthah acted in character in seeking an amicable settlement, and finds nothing in that inconsistent with a man of valour.

Henry makes most of the delay, since it shows Jephthah would not compel by the sword what he could gain by reason, war being the last remedy and the same rule holding for going to law; he doubts the claim was ever the real reason, thinking the Ammonites came for plunder and searched old musty records only when they could not for shame own what they had come for, and observes that even men who do the greatest wrong wish to seem in the right.

Clarke reads a colder motive into the embassy, that by making the Ammonites state their own grounds Jephthah would let the justice of his cause appear the more forcibly to his people, and notes that Moab appears to have been confederate with Ammon in this war.

Ellicott compares the proceeding to the Roman practice of sending heralds ahead of a war, calls the Ammonite plea plausible but not in accordance with the facts, and says it was absurd to expect Israel to shed its blood for settlements only to hand them back to neighbours who hated it; he fixes the Arnon and the Jabbok as the bounds of Gad and Reuben. Keil and Delitzsch note that the ambassadors speak in the name of the nation, and allow the claim one feature with a certain colour of justice, since part of what Israel held had once been Moabite.

themes: what hast thou to do with me
Israel took away my land
from Arnon even unto Jabbok
restore those lands again peaceably

14.pericope_label: The march from Egypt and the war with Sihon

schools.summary: Gill supplies the fear behind Sihon's refusal, that he knew his people were of the seven nations whose land Israel was going to take, makes Heshbon weigh in the dispute since Sihon had taken it from Moab, and draws the conclusion Jephthah is working towards, that Israel holds the land by a divine right because the victory was the Lord's.
Clarke marks the bounds of what was won, from Arabia Deserta on the east to the Jordan on the west.

Ellicott sees no difficulty in Jephthah's knowing the history, since even without documents the events were not so old as to have been forgotten, glosses the geography as he goes, and observes that the conquest east of Jordan was never part of Israel's plan but was forced on them by the hostility of Sihon and Og; Keil and Delitzsch note that the rehearsal agrees exactly with the Pentateuch, that these verses stand almost word for word as in Numbers, and that the embassy to Moab is nowhere recorded in the books of Moses, having had no bearing on the course Israel took.

themes: Israel took not away the land of Moab
the king of Edom would not hearken
let us pass through thy land
Sihon trusted not Israel

23.pericope_label: Chemosh, Balak, and three hundred years

schools.summary: Gill calls the appeal to Chemosh an argument put to the man on his own ground, and thinks the comparison with Balak strengthens the guess that the king Jephthah addressed ruled Moab as well as Ammon.

Clarke sets out the chain of title — the Ammonites lost the land to the Amorites, Israel conquered it from the Amorites, God granted it, and Ammon never reclaimed it because the title was good — and reads the appeal to Chemosh as an argument from a maxim both sides held, that what a nation's god has given it may keep; he takes the three hundred years at face value and makes undisturbed possession part of the case.

Ellicott notes that Chemosh was distinctively the god of Moab and Moloch of Ammon, so the phrase shows how closely the two kindred nations were joined, and hears a possible echo of the old song of triumph over Heshbon; he doubts the three hundred years belong to the text at all, finding them irreconcilable with the preserved genealogies, needless to the argument, and in conflict with the rest of the sentence. Keil and Delitzsch see the appeal to Balak as a second proof designed to strip the claim of its last appearance of right, and close with Jephthah leaving the matter to Jehovah the Judge.

debates.question: Are the three hundred years part of the original text?

sides.position: doubtful — probably a marginal gloss, since the number cannot be reconciled with the genealogies and is needless to the argument
genuine, and one of the strongest points in the case, undisturbed possession for that length of time

themes: that which Chemosh thy god giveth thee
art thou any thing better than Balak
three hundred years
the Lord the Judge be judge this day

29.pericope_label: The Spirit of the Lord, and the vow

schools.summary: Gill glosses the Spirit from the Targum as the spirit of strength, such as was given when God raised men up to deliver Israel, and sees in it a change of office, since Jephthah had been chosen general by the eastern tribes but was now qualified as judge of all Israel.

Henry has the Spirit come only when the people's choice had shown a clear call and Ammon's deafness a just cause, and reads even the route as evidence of the discretion it gave; on the vow he finds remainders of distrust in the hearts of true and great believers, since Jephthah still hesitates when it comes to the settling, and suspects the snare was meant to correct that weakness and the conceit that victory must be bought with something considerable.
Clarke reads the Spirit as a testimony rather than an equipment, God qualifying him for the work and so declaring his cause good.

Ellicott would render the verb went through rather than passed over, the object being to collect levies and rouse the tribes, and notes that vowing was a practice of all ancient nations and particularly of the Jews; Keil and Delitzsch quote the terms of the vow exactly and close off the softer reading, since the phrase about coming out of the doors of the house to meet a man will not describe a beast driven from the stall or one that happens to run out, being used everywhere else of people.

themes: the Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah
he passed over Mizpeh of Gilead
if thou shalt without fail deliver them
whatsoever cometh forth of the doors of my house

schools.summary: Gill states the fork plainly: if to meet me is meant of intention, none but a human creature can be intended, since nothing else could come out by design; if it means only what happened to meet him, any creature may be. He fixes the terms narrowly on whatever came out first, as the Latin has it, since at such a moment many might come out at once.

Clarke holds that conditions must have been implied, since without them the vow would be that of a heathen or a madman, presses the character of a man who could not commit the crime he had just punished in others, offers a conjecture that a lost letter turned I will offer Him a burnt offering into I will offer it up for a burnt offering, and concludes from the end of the chapter that the daughter was consecrated to perpetual virginity rather than sacrificed.

Ellicott answers every one of these arguments: the rendering is whosoever and not whatsoever, the marginal or comes of the same wish to soften the verse, the animal reading is a notion Augustine ridiculed and a strangely inadequate return besides, and human sacrifice was the special worship of the very nations Jephthah was marching against; to the objection from the Spirit he replies that the Spirit clothed Gideon who set up an illegal worship, came on Saul who was ready to kill his own son over a vow, and came on David who sank into adultery and murder, the phrase being a grant of strength for a particular end and not a certificate of attainment. Keil and Delitzsch, having shut off the reading that makes the victim a beast, pass straight from the vow to the battle.

debates.question: Did Jephthah vow a human sacrifice?

sides.position: yes — the rendering is whosoever, a single beast would be an absurd return, and the practice was common among the nations he had lived and fought among
no — conditions must have been implied, the man was pious and knew the law, and the close of the chapter shows the daughter consecrated to virginity

outliers.note: Meets the argument from the Spirit of the Lord head on, holding that the phrase marks divine strength granted for a particular end and proves nothing about the character of the man who receives it.

themes: whatsoever cometh forth to meet me
shall surely be the Lord’s
I will offer it up for a burnt offering
whether a human sacrifice was meant

32.pericope_label: The victory, the meeting, and the daughter's consent

schools.summary: Gill notes that Jephthah returned to the Mizpeh where he had spoken his terms before the Lord and had settled the family he brought out of Tob, and observes that the daughter does not say if thou hast opened thy mouth, since her father had plainly told her what he had vowed.

Clarke reads the twenty cities as either taken or destroyed, takes the father's grief to be for a family now extinct in Israel rather than for a death, calls the daughter at once obedient, pious and patriotic, and notes what her consent cost, since to have no offspring was the utmost degradation among the Hebrews; on her two months he supposes she went no further than a farewell visit to each of her companions.

Ellicott points out that the word opening the battle is simply and, not so, and does not connect the victory to the vow, explains that a vow was binding only when spoken and that the Hebrews knew a redeemable vow and an irredeemable ban, and holds that Jephthah treated his as a ban and never thought of escaping it; he will not defend the theology, quoting Josephus that the sacrifice was neither lawful nor acceptable to God, but praises the faithfulness that would not go back and the devotion of the daughter, and explains that what she went to bewail was not death but dying unwedded and childless. Keil and Delitzsch fix the ground of the battle from Aroer to Minnith and Abel of the vineyards.

themes: the Lord delivered them into his hands
his daughter came out with timbrels and dances
I have opened my mouth unto the Lord
bewail my virginity upon the mountains

schools.summary: Gill lays out the choices without deciding: some take the verb of lamenting her death and some of her virginity, but it may mean to talk with her and hold conversation, as two of the rabbis understood it, the daughters bringing her news to cheer her in her solitude; he adds a third possibility from the Arabic, where the root means to praise, and notes that this book uses it so of rehearsing the righteous acts of the Lord.

Clarke says flatly that to lament is not a correct translation, gives a rendering in which the virgins go to comfort her, and uses the verse as evidence that she was alive to be comforted; he then sets out at length the exposition that turns the vow into two by reading the conjunction disjunctively, supports it from the Levitical law of vows with its three subjects for three uses, and makes the daughter irredeemably devoted, but to perpetual virginity in the service of the tabernacle — a service he says was already customary, since a tribute of thirty-two captive virgins had gone to the Lord after the Midianite war.

Ellicott reports the same sense of the verb from a rabbi, taking it as praise or celebration, and compares what the Romans felt for Claelia, or any nation for a heroine whose self-sacrifice bought it a victory.

debates.question: What did the daughters of Israel go yearly to do?

sides.position: to comfort her, which shows she was living — to lament is not a correct translation
to praise or celebrate her, as the Arabic root and a rabbinic reading both allow

themes: the daughters of Israel went yearly
four days in a year
to lament, or to praise
the custom in Israel
